content: Yale-New Haven Hospital (YNHH) is a prestigious 944-bed medical facility located in downtown New Haven, Connecticut. It is owned and operated by the Yale New Haven Health System, Inc. The hospital includes the 201-bed Yale-New Haven Children’s Hospital and the 76-bed Yale-New Haven Psychiatric Hospital. YNHH serves as the primary teaching hospital for the Yale University School of Medicine and is accredited by the Joint Commission on the Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations (JCAHO). It has been ranked by U.S. News & World Report as the 15th-best hospital out of 5,462 medical centers in the United States. The hospital is recognized as being among the best in 10 of the 16 medical specialties evaluated, including cancer, digestive disorders, ear, nose, and throat, endocrinology, gynecology, heart and heart surgery, kidney disease, psychiatry, respiratory disorders, and urology. Its geriatrics and psychiatry departments are ranked in the nation’s top 10, while specialties such as gynecology, digestive disorders, endocrinology, kidney disorders, respiratory disorders, and oncology are ranked in the top 25. The hospital provides care to over 503,000 outpatient and emergency visits annually and handles 50,000 inpatient discharges per year. It is the second-largest employer in New Haven, Connecticut, with approximately 6,000 employees and a physician base of over 2,200 university-affiliated and community physicians practicing in more than 100 medical specialties. History The history of Yale-New Haven Hospital dates back to 1826 when the General Hospital Society of Connecticut was chartered as the first hospital in Connecticut and the fourth voluntary hospital in the United States. The hospital initially operated in temporary quarters and raised $5,000 to purchase land and construct a facility. In 1833, a new 13-bed hospital opened on a 7.5-acre site bordered by Cedar Street, Howard Avenue, Davenport Avenue, and Congress Avenue. The original building, known as the State Hospital, was designed by prominent New Haven architect Ithiel Town and cost $13,000. During the American Civil War in 1862, the hospital was converted into a military hospital to care for Union soldiers and renamed the Knight United States Army General Hospital in honor of Jonathan Knight, the president of the board of trustees. Some attending physicians relocated with civilian patients to temporary quarters on Whitney Avenue. After the Civil War, the hospital was returned to the General Society of Connecticut in 1865 and reverted to its original name, State Hospital. In 1873, the hospital opened the Connecticut Training School, the third training school for nurses in the United States. In 1884, the hospital’s name was changed to New Haven Hospital to reflect the name commonly used by local residents. In 1913, Yale School of Medicine and New Haven Hospital formalized their relationship, marking the beginning of what is now known as the Yale-New Haven Medical Center. This partnership evolved from a simple apprenticeship system to a formal educational alliance between medical schools and hospitals. In 1914, the hospital purchased its first motorized ambulance. In 1945, the hospital was renamed Grace-New Haven Hospital after affiliating with nearby Grace Hospital. In 1951, the New Haven Dispensary, the city’s first outpatient clinic established in 1871, formally merged with Grace-New Haven Hospital. In 1965, a more formal agreement with the Yale School of Medicine resulted in another name change to Yale-New Haven Hospital. In 1993, the Yale-New Haven Children’s Hospital opened, becoming the first full-service children’s hospital in Connecticut, including the state’s first children’s emergency department. In 2000, the Yale-New Haven Psychiatric Hospital was established following the acquisition of the Yale Psychiatric Institute. Today, YNHH is a 944-bed private, nonprofit facility that ranks among the premier medical centers in the nation. It is the largest acute care provider in southern Connecticut and one of the Northeast’s major referral centers. Physical Plant The main patient campus of Yale-New Haven Hospital consists of three inpatient pavilions bounded by South Frontage Road, Park Street, Howard Avenue, and York Street. The East Pavilion, originally called the Memorial Unit, opened in 1950 and was designed by architect Douglas Orr. The South Pavilion opened in 1982, followed by the Yale-New Haven Children’s Hospital (West Pavilion) in 1993. All three pavilions are connected by a central atrium. In 2000, YNHH acquired the nearby Yale Psychiatric Institute, designed by architect Frank Gehry in 1989, and opened the Yale-New Haven Psychiatric Hospital. In 2004, the Yale-New Haven Shoreline Medical Center in Guilford, Connecticut, was opened. The New Haven Pavilion houses outpatient clinics, clinical laboratories, administration, and other departments. Located across the street from the inpatient pavilions, it occupies the site of the original hospital built in 1833. The New Haven Pavilion connects directly to facilities of the Yale School of Medicine. New Cancer Center Building In 2004, Yale-New Haven Hospital proposed constructing a new $430-million building for the Yale Cancer Center, a Comprehensive Cancer Center. Although construction was scheduled to begin in September 2005, the project was delayed due to disputes with unions and the city. On March 22, 2006, an agreement was reached between the unions and the hospital. Construction of the new Yale-New Haven Cancer Hospital began on May 18, 2006, with the demolition of the Grace Building and site preparation. Groundbreaking occurred on September 6, 2006. The new Cancer Center building, also known as the North Pavilion, will be connected to the other facilities via the atrium. The building is scheduled to open in 2009.
